Divides the 3 V by the 2 Ω resistor, ignoring the other branches.

questions.topic: Kirchhoff's Laws and the Wheatstone Bridge
questions.question: A bridge has P = 1 Ω (A to B), Q = 2 Ω (B to C), R = 2 Ω (A to D) and S = 1 Ω (D to C), with a zero-resistance galvanometer between B and D. An ideal 6 V battery is across A and C. What current flows through the galvanometer?
questions.explanation:
With zero galvanometer resistance, B and D are one node. P, R in parallel give \( \tfrac{2}{3} \) Ω; Q, S in parallel give \( \tfrac{2}{3} \) Ω.

Each pair has 3 V across it: \( I_P=3 \) A, \( I_Q=1.5 \) A.

Junction B: galvanometer current \( =3-1.5=1.5 \) A.
questions.hint: Check the balance condition first; if it fails, use junction currents.
distractor_logic: Assumes the bridge is balanced; here P/Q is not equal to R/S.
Reports the total battery current.
Reports the current in P or S instead of the difference at the junction.

questions.topic: Kirchhoff's Laws and the Wheatstone Bridge
questions.question: In a meter bridge, X is in the left gap and 10 Ω in the right gap; the null point is at 60 cm. A 30 Ω resistor is then connected in parallel with X. Where is the new null point?
questions.explanation:
\( X=10\times\dfrac{60}{40}=15 \) Ω.

With 30 Ω in parallel: \( \dfrac{15\times30}{45}=10 \) Ω.

Equal resistances in both gaps: balance at \( 50 \) cm.
questions.hint: Find X first, then the new left-gap resistance.
distractor_logic: Assumes the null point does not move when X is changed.
Puts the new balance on the wrong side of the wire.
Takes the new left resistance as 30 Ω alone, ignoring X.

questions.topic: Kirchhoff's Laws and the Wheatstone Bridge
questions.question: A balanced bridge with P = 2 Ω, Q = 4 Ω, R = 3 Ω, S = 6 Ω is fed by a cell of EMF 7.2 V and internal resistance 0.4 Ω. What current does the cell supply?
questions.hint: Balance lets you drop the galvanometer, not the internal resistance.
distractor_logic: Ignores the cell's internal resistance; balance does not depend on it, but the current does.
Confuses zero galvanometer current with zero battery current.
Puts all four arms and the internal resistance in series.

questions.topic: Kirchhoff's Laws and the Wheatstone Bridge
questions.question: In a meter bridge experiment, the known resistance is chosen so that the null point lies near the middle of the wire. Why?
options: The galvanometer's resistance cancels only when balance is at the middle
The battery's internal resistance cancels only at the middle
The current in the wire is maximum at the middle
It reduces the effect of end resistances and the percentage error in reading lengths
questions.explanation:
The balance condition holds anywhere on the wire, independent of galvanometer and battery resistances.

But extra resistance at the wire ends and reading errors affect short lengths most, so a near-middle balance gives the smallest percentage error.
questions.hint: Which errors grow when one of the two lengths is small?
distractor_logic: The galvanometer's resistance never enters the balance condition, wherever the null point is.
The battery's resistance never affects the balance condition.
The wire carries the same current along its whole length.

questions.topic: The Potentiometer and Its Applications
questions.question: A cell balances at 150 cm on open circuit and at 120 cm when shunted by 8 Ω. The potential gradient is 0.01 V/cm. What current flows through the shunt when it is connected?
questions.hint: Find the EMF and internal resistance first.
distractor_logic: Ignores the internal resistance, dividing the EMF by 8 Ω alone.
Divides the EMF by the internal resistance only.
Confuses zero galvanometer current at balance with zero current in the shunt.

questions.topic: The Potentiometer and Its Applications
questions.question: Two cells in series balance at 90 cm when their EMFs aid each other and at 30 cm when they oppose. What is the ratio of the larger EMF to the smaller?
questions.explanation:
\( \varepsilon_1+\varepsilon_2\propto90 \), \( \varepsilon_1-\varepsilon_2\propto30 \).

\( \dfrac{\varepsilon_1}{\varepsilon_2}=\dfrac{90+30}{90-30}=\dfrac{120}{60}=2 \).
questions.hint: Add and subtract the two conditions.
distractor_logic: Takes the ratio of the two balancing lengths directly.
Inverts the ratio.
Divides the sum of lengths by the opposing length only.

questions.topic: The Potentiometer and Its Applications
questions.question: Resistors R1 = 10 Ω and R2 are in series with a steady current. On a potentiometer, the drop across R1 balances at 40 cm and the drop across R1 and R2 together balances at 100 cm. Find R2.
questions.hint: The drop is proportional to resistance when the current is the same.
distractor_logic: Uses 100/40 for R2 instead of for R1 + R2.
Multiplies R1 by 40/100.
Multiplies R1 by 60/100.

questions.topic: The Potentiometer and Its Applications
questions.question: A driver cell of EMF 3 V and internal resistance 2 Ω is in series with a 3 Ω rheostat and a 5 m potentiometer wire of resistance 5 Ω. Where does a 0.6 V cell balance?
questions.hint: Include every resistance in the driver circuit.
distractor_logic: Ignores the driver cell's internal resistance.
Divides the gradient by the EMF instead of the reverse.
Reads the result in metres as centimetres.

questions.topic: The Potentiometer and Its Applications
questions.question: A cell's EMF is being measured with a potentiometer. The galvanometer in the cell's branch is replaced by one with a much larger resistance. What happens to the balancing length?
options: It increases, since more resistance is in the cell branch
No balance can be found any more
questions.explanation:
At balance, no current flows through the galvanometer or the test cell.

With zero current, the galvanometer's resistance causes no drop, so the balancing length is unchanged (only the sensitivity near balance changes).
questions.hint: What current flows through the galvanometer at the null point?
distractor_logic: At the null point no current flows in that branch, so its resistance has no effect.
Assumes a drop across the galvanometer; there is none at balance.
The null condition depends only on EMF and gradient.

questions.topic: The Potentiometer and Its Applications
questions.question: On a potentiometer, a cell balances at 240 cm on open circuit and at 200 cm when shunted by 4 Ω. If the shunt is replaced by 3.2 Ω, where is the new balance point?
questions.explanation:
\( r=4\left(\dfrac{240}{200}-1\right)=0.8 \) Ω.

New terminal voltage fraction \( =\dfrac{3.2}{3.2+0.8}=0.8 \).

\( l=0.8\times240=192 \) cm.
questions.hint: First extract the internal resistance.
distractor_logic: Assumes the balance length does not depend on the shunt value.
Takes the open-circuit (EMF) length.
Scales the old shunted length instead of the EMF length.

questions.topic: Electric Current, Drift Velocity, and Ohm's Law
questions.question: A wire is replaced by one of the same material and length but twice the radius, and the same current is maintained. How do the drift speed and the resistance change?
options: Drift speed becomes one-fourth; resistance is unchanged
Drift speed is unchanged; resistance becomes one-fourth
questions.explanation:
Area becomes 4 times.

\( v_d=\dfrac{I}{neA} \): one-fourth. \( R=\rho\dfrac{L}{A} \): one-fourth, while \( \rho \) itself is unchanged.
questions.hint: Both quantities depend on the area.
distractor_logic: Treats resistance like resistivity, as if it did not depend on area.
Scales with the radius instead of the area.
Forgets that the same current spread over a larger area drifts more slowly.

questions.topic: Electric Current, Drift Velocity, and Ohm's Law
questions.question: A 1 m wire of resistivity \( 10^{-8} \) Ω m has \( n=10^{29} \) \( \text{m}^{-3} \) and \( 0.016 \) V across it. Taking \( e=1.6\times10^{-19} \) C, what is the drift speed \( v_d \)?
questions.explanation:
Combine \( j=\dfrac{E}{\rho} \) and \( j=nev_d \): \( v_d=\dfrac{V}{\rho neL} \).

\( \rho neL=10^{-8}\times10^{29}\times1.6\times10^{-19}\times1=160 \)

\( v_d=\dfrac{0.016}{160}=10^{-4} \) m/s.
questions.hint: Link the field to current density through resistivity.
distractor_logic: Inverts the expression for drift speed.
Leaves the resistivity out of the calculation.
Confuses drift speed with the speed at which the field is set up.

questions.topic: Electric Current, Drift Velocity, and Ohm's Law
questions.question: A metal wire is connected across a fixed voltage and then heated. What happens to the current and to the drift speed of its electrons?
